subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
The first big idea is decomposition — a long word for a simple habit. When a job is too big to do all at once, we split it into smaller pieces called sub-tasks. Making a whole game is a big job, but “what the cat does when the game starts” is a small job, and “what the mouse does when you click it” is another. Each small job is easy to plan and to fix on its own.

The second big idea is that programmers learn from their mistakes. A mistake in a program is called an error or a bug, and bugs are completely normal — even the best programmers make them all day long. What matters is that we do not panic; we find the bug, fix it, and remember it. The third big idea, testing and debugging, is how we do that. To test means to run a program and check it does the right thing; to debug means to find the wrong part and fix it.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 3 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Break a big task into smaller sub-tasks (decomposition).
Understand that each sub-task can have its own algorithm and its own code, and can be planned and fixed on its own.
Understand that mistakes (errors or bugs) are a normal part of programming, and that we learn from them.
Test a program by running it and checking it against the plan.
Debug a program: find the part that is wrong, change it, and test again.
In Scratch, build event-driven code for more than one sprite (green flag, when clicked, when a key is pressed) using movement, costume and sound blocks.
Plan, build, test and debug a simple two-sprite chase game.

concepts.title: Breaking a big task into sub-tasks
concepts.explanation:
Some jobs are too big to think about all at once. We can break a big job into smaller jobs called sub-tasks. Each sub-task is easier to plan, easier to do, and easier to fix. Breaking a big job into smaller jobs is called decomposition.

Getting ready for school is a big job, but we do not do it all in one go. We break it into smaller jobs: pack your bag, put on clean clothes, find your shoes, walk to school.
concepts.example: Each one is a sub-task, and doing them all finishes the big job. Start with something you know.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you name sensible sub-tasks — smaller than the whole job, but bigger than a single tiny step? Do not worry about perfect wording; the thinking is what matters.

concepts.title: Sub-tasks in a game: events start the code
concepts.explanation:
In a Scratch game, each sub-task is started by an event — something that happens. The three events we use are: the green flag is clicked (the game starts), a sprite is clicked on, and a key is pressed. Each event runs its own little algorithm. So one sprite can have more than one sub-task, each with a different starting event.

Think about a light switch. Flicking it up turns the light on; flicking it down turns it off.
concepts.example: Same light, two events, two different jobs. Our cat is the same: the green flag makes it say hello, but clicking it makes it move.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you see that one sprite can have more than one sub-task? In your game plan, are the ideas simple enough to actually build (move, say, costume, sound)?

concepts.title: Mistakes, errors and being a bug detective
concepts.explanation:
Programs often have mistakes. A mistake in a program is called an error or a bug. Bugs are normal — every programmer makes them. We do not feel bad about a bug; we become a detective, find it, and fix it. Finding a bug even helps us, because we learn something and remember it next time.

A computer does exactly what your blocks say — not what you meant, but what you said. If a block is wrong, the computer still does it and you get a surprise.
concepts.example: That surprise is a bug. It is not your fault and not the computer being naughty — it just means one block needs fixing.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you trace the code to test it rather than guessing? Can you point to the exact wrong block and say what it should be? Does you stay calm and curious about a bug?

concepts.title: Build and test the cat in Scratch
concepts.explanation:
Now we build the two-sub-task cat from Session 2 on the computer, and we learn to test it — to run it and check it does what we planned. If it does not, we debug it.

A new project already has the cat sprite, so we do not need to add one. Open Scratch at scratch.mit.edu and click Create on the projector.
concepts.example: Remind you of the screen: the coloured blocks on the left, the script area in the middle where we join them, and the stage on the top right where it happens. Choose a simple backdrop like Blue Sky.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you start each sub-task with the correct hat block, click to test, and say whether it matched the plan? Can you find a block by its colour group and join it to the right stack?

concepts.title: The chase game: controls, a second sprite, and debugging
concepts.explanation:
We turn our project into a real chase game. We add controls so the player can move the cat with the arrow keys, and we add a second sprite — a mouse — that runs away when you click it. Then we test and debug the whole thing.

Set the scene: “At Ehel Academy, a cheeky mouse has grabbed a date from the snack tray! Help Leila's cat chase the mouse.” Start a new project.
concepts.example: The cat is already there; add the Mouse1 sprite with the Add Sprite button. Choose the Forest backdrop (or Blue Sky).
concepts.checkYourself: Can you test by running, notice when something does not match the plan, and try a fix? Can you build several small sub-tasks and keep you separate, each with the correct hat block?

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

The most important one to fix. Bugs are normal and every programmer gets them. Show your own bugs cheerfully so a mistake feels like a puzzle, not a failure.
The computer always does exactly what the blocks say. The bug is in our blocks, which puts you in charge of the fix.
All the code for a sprite goes in one big stack.
Different events need different hat blocks and separate stacks. Clicking a sprite and clicking the green flag are two sub-tasks, not one.
A sub-task is the same as one tiny step.
A sub-task is a small job (like
what the cat does when clicked

) that itself has several steps. It sits between the whole task and a single instruction. Forgetting the minus sign. change x by (10) moves right; change x by (-10) moves left. A dropped minus sign sends a sprite the wrong way — a very common chase-game bug.
If it runs without an error message, it must be right.
A program can run perfectly and still do the wrong thing (the cat grows when it should shrink). Always test against the plan, not just for crashes.

selfAssessment: I can break a big task into smaller sub-tasks (decomposition).
I can understand that each sub-task can have its own algorithm and its own code, and can be planned and fixed on its own.
I can understand that mistakes (errors or bugs) are a normal part of programming, and that we learn from them.
I can test a program by running it and checking it against the plan.
I can debug a program: find the part that is wrong, change it, and test again.
I can in Scratch, build event-driven code for more than one sprite (green flag, when clicked, when a key is pressed) using movement, costume and sound blocks.
I can plan, build, test and debug a simple two-sprite chase game.
